forces: Orchestra with offstage oboe and four timpanists
intro: Scène aux champs, the Adagio third movement of the Symphonie fantastique, Op. 14, opens with a cor anglais call to a distant oboe, representing two shepherds at the end of the day. When the call returns, the oboe does not reply and only thunder follows.

sections.label: Intro · Cor anglais and distant oboe
A · Flute and violins in F
sections.mNote: A long pastoral melody begins in unison.

sections.label: B · The beloved disturbs the countryside
sections.mNote: Wind phrases and restless strings lead towards the idée fixe.

sections.label: A′ · Pastoral theme returns
sections.mNote: Woodwinds play the theme over pizzicato strings.

sections.label: Intro′ · Cor anglais alone, distant thunder
sections.mNote: Cor anglais and distant thunder; the oboe does not reply.

cues.title: Opening dialogue, cor anglais and oboe
cues.text: A cor anglais and a distant oboe exchange slow phrases. The oboe is marked lontano (far away). In Berlioz’s programme the two players are shepherds, and at first they play without accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Movement III, opening bars, Michel Austin’s score transcription: http://www.hberlioz.com/scosupp/symfantas3.pdf . Berlioz’s programme identifies the two players as shepherds.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Composition of the Adagio
cues.text: This Adagio cost Berlioz more than three weeks of work, and he put it aside and returned to it two or three times. In his Mémoires he set this against the march to the scaffold, which he wrote in a single night.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter 26, on composing the third and fourth movements: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

cues.title: Principal theme, flute and violins
cues.text: The flute and first violins play a broad melody in F major in unison. Plucked strings join beneath them.
cues.evidence: Movement III, principal theme from bar 20, with plucked string accompaniment joining at bar 24; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 2–3.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Berlioz’s programme, third movement
cues.text: In Berlioz’s programme, the evening, the shepherds’ ranz des vaches, trees stirred lightly by the wind and a few new hopes bring the artist “an unaccustomed calm”. He thinks of his isolation and hopes not to be alone much longer.
cues.evidence: Berlioz’s programme, part III, in both the 1845 and 1855 versions (“un calme inaccoutumé”): http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

cues.title: Allusions to Beethoven’s birdsong
cues.text: F major is the key of Beethoven’s “Pastoral” Symphony, and this scene is an homage to it. From bar 67, after the main melody, there are discreet allusions to the birdsong that closes the “Pastoral”’s slow movement.
cues.evidence: Michel Austin’s commentary on movement III: the movement recalls the Pastoral Symphony in the same key, with intentional echoes of its bird song from bar 67: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm

cues.title: Central episode, idée fixe
cues.text: The middle episode has shorter wind phrases, and the strings grow more restless. The idée fixe enters in the woodwinds and, in altered form, in the basses (bars 87–102). In Berlioz’s programme the artist fears at this point that his beloved is deceiving him.
cues.evidence: Movement III, central episode, including the idée fixe at bars 87–102; score and commentary: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm . The fear of betrayal appears in Berlioz’s programme, part III.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Solo clarinet over pizzicato strings
cues.text: The pastoral music returns at Tempo I, and the woodwinds play quietly. From bar 119 a solo clarinet takes the tune above pizzicato second violins and divided violas. The flute echoes it, and the strings continue pizzicato.
cues.evidence: Movement III, bars 110–123: Tempo I, quiet woodwind phrases, pizzicato accompaniment and solo clarinet from bar 119. Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 21–22.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Borrowing from the Messe solennelle
cues.text: The pastoral tune first appeared in the Gratias of Berlioz’s Messe solennelle, written in 1824–25. Berlioz moved it from E major to F major for the symphony. The Mass was lost for generations, and the borrowing became known only when it was rediscovered in 1991.
cues.evidence: Hector Berlioz Website, Symphonie fantastique, composition history and third-movement commentary: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm

cues.title: Revision after the 1830 première
cues.text: At the première in December 1830 this movement made little impression, and Berlioz resolved to rewrite it. His friend Ferdinand Hiller offered advice. The long countryside scene was among the revisions Berlioz made over several years.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter 31, on the third movement’s reception and Hiller’s advice; chapter 26, on revisions over several years: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

cues.title: Cor anglais and four timpani
cues.text: The cor anglais plays its call again, and the distant oboe does not reply. Beneath it, four timpanists play rolls that rise and fade to represent thunder. Berlioz asked for soft sponge-headed sticks.
cues.evidence: Movement III, bars 175–196; the score specifies four timpanists and baguettes d’éponge. Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 37–38. The unanswered call and thunder are named in the programme.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Programme text, 1855 version
cues.text: Berlioz ended this scene in his 1855 programme with a few broken phrases: “The sun goes down … distant thunder … solitude … silence.” In the programme, the second shepherd does not reply.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, programme of Symphonie fantastique, 1855 version, part III. Our translation of “Le soleil se couche… bruit éloigné du tonnerre… solitude… silence…”: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

cues.title: Programme for part IV, 1845
cues.text: After the silence, the 1845 programme turns to the artist’s despair. Sure that his love is unrecognised, he takes opium. The dose is too weak to kill him but brings strange visions, in which he is led to the scaffold.
cues.evidence: Berlioz’s 1845 programme, part IV, Marche au supplice (“l’artiste s’empoisonne avec de l’opium”): http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

transitions.title: Flute and violins begin the principal tune
transitions.from: Intro · Cor anglais and distant oboe
transitions.to: A · Flute and violins in F
transitions.how: The shepherds’ exchange ends. Flute and first violins begin the principal tune in F major, in unison and with little else sounding. Second violins, violas, cellos and basses enter beneath the melody, pizzicato. The Adagio tempo continues.
transitions.evidence: Movement III, bars 20–28; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 2–3.

transitions.title: The pastoral tune breaks into fragments
transitions.from: A · Flute and violins in F
transitions.to: B · The beloved disturbs the countryside
transitions.how: The F major pastoral tune is followed by short wind phrases. The strings climb, adding chromatic notes and repeated figures, marked crescendo poco a poco at bar 83. From bar 87 bassoons, cellos and basses play a distorted form of the idée fixe beneath tremolo chords in the violins.
transitions.evidence: Movement III, approach to the central episode and bars 81–102, especially the crescendo at bar 83 and bass-line idée fixe from bar 87; Michel Austin’s score transcription.

transitions.title: Return to Tempo I, bars 110–123
transitions.from: B · The beloved disturbs the countryside
transitions.how: The agitated phrases slow in a rallentando and fade. At Tempo I, flute and oboes play against a sustained note in the solo cellos. The pastoral tune returns in a solo clarinet with a new accompaniment beneath it: pizzicato semiquavers in second violins and divided violas, marked pianississimo.
transitions.evidence: Movement III, bars 110–123, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 21–22: rallentando, Tempo I, solo cellos and pizzicato accompaniment.

transitions.title: Cor anglais returns without the oboe
transitions.to: Intro′ · Cor anglais alone, distant thunder
transitions.how: The F major pastoral music thins to plucked strings and quiet wind chords. At un poco ritenuto the cor anglais takes over. It plays the opening call again, this time with no reply from the distant oboe. Beneath it the timpani, tuned to B♭, F, A♭ and C, play rolls.
transitions.evidence: Movement III, bars 171–182, Michel Austin’s score transcription, p. 37; the timpani parts specify the four pitches.

source.title: Berlioz, Scène aux champs — orchestral score
source.locator: Shepherds’ calls, bars 1–20; pastoral theme from bar 20; central idée fixe, bars 87–102; returning call and thunder, bars 175–196; final string chords, bars 197–199.

timeline.note: Cor anglais and distant oboe exchange unaccompanied calls.
Muted, divided violas join the shepherds’ calls.
Flute and first violins play the pastoral tune, with pizzicato strings beneath them.
Woodwinds and strings exchange the pastoral tune and its accompanying figures.
Short wind phrases lead into rising string figures and the idée fixe.
Quiet woodwind phrases give way to a solo clarinet above plucked second violins and violas.
The cor anglais plays alone; four timpanists follow with distant thunder.
The cor anglais continues between soft, overlapping timpani rolls.
The thunder fades; quiet horns and bowed strings close in F major.

composer.background:
When the young Hector Berlioz read aloud the death of Dido, his voice failed him. His father closed the book and said that he was tired, so the boy did not have to explain his tears. Berlioz recorded the kindness in his Mémoires. Louis Berlioz was a doctor in La Côte-Saint-André, between Lyon and Grenoble, and taught his son Latin, history and geography. He expected Hector to follow him into medicine. The boy learnt the flute and guitar, studied maps of distant islands and was deeply moved by the story of Virgil’s abandoned queen.

In 1821 he went to Paris to study medicine. His first visit to the dissecting room at the Pitié hospital, he later wrote, ended with a flight through a window. On the second visit he managed perfectly well. Music was the more durable obstacle. He heard Salieri’s Les Danaïdes at the Opéra and began singing its airs over the cadavers. At the Conservatoire library he copied and memorised Gluck’s scores. His father argued, threatened and withheld support. Hector took composition lessons with Jean-François Le Sueur.
